Dear Anu,

You asked about hostel life. Forget hostel life. There is a boy in my economics tutorial called Hemant, and I think I might be in trouble.

He is the funniest person I've ever met. Yesterday the professor's microphone died and Hemant did the rest of the lecture in a perfect radio-announcer voice until even the professor laughed. He walks into class like he owns it.

We've talked exactly three times. Once about the canteen samosas, once about a film, once about nothing. And I already know what our flat would look like. Books everywhere. A cat. He would make me laugh every morning.

I know. I KNOW. I don't even know his surname. But you should see how he smiles when he's about to say something ridiculous.

Don't tell Amma.

Your didi,
Kavitha

qa.a: Exactly three times.

qa.q: How does Kavitha feel about Hemant, and what does the imagined flat show?
qa.a: She feels excited and infatuated; imagining their flat after three talks shows she is filling in the blanks with a future she wishes for.

qa.a: Enjoy the crush, but get to know Hemant slowly beyond his jokes, so she learns who he really is rather than who she imagines.

grounding: Kavitha is drawn to Hemant's humour and confidence and imagines a whole future from three conversations, showing infatuation filling in the blanks.

So you want the embarrassing story? Fine. I'm Raghav, second year, and last month I was completely gone over a girl called Gurleen.

She was in my debate society. She stood up on the first day and destroyed the opposing team with one joke, and everyone was laughing, even them. I thought, that's it, that's the one.

We spoke maybe four times after practice. She liked old Hindi songs. That was enough. In my head we were already travelling to Spiti together, she was meeting my parents, we had inside jokes.

Then one evening I heard her talk about wanting to move abroad after college and never come back, and I felt this jolt. Because I'd never asked. I'd just decided who she was. The Gurleen in my head was mostly me, with her face on.

qa.a: Old Hindi songs.

qa.a: He feels surprised and a little foolish, realising he had imagined who she was without ever asking.

qa.a: He could get to know Gurleen through real conversations, asking about her plans and values, instead of imagining them.

qa.a: She might feel flattered but also uneasy, since she barely knows Raghav and he had pictured a future for her.

grounding: Raghav is drawn to Gurleen's humour and confidence and imagines a future from a few chats, until he realises the person he saw was partly wished for.

Okay, I'm Darshan, and I'll admit it. I watched Kiran's story from the hiking trip eleven times.

Not in a creepy way. I just wanted to find the right thing to reply. I typed "Wow!" and deleted it. Too boring. Typed "Next time take me!" and deleted it. Too much. Finally I sent a mountain emoji. Then I stared at my phone.

She replied in four minutes. Four. I screenshotted it and sent it to my roommate.

Two days later I asked her for coffee. I rehearsed it in the mirror, very casual: "If you're free sometime..." She took three hours to reply and I was convinced she hated me. Turns out she was in a lab.

The thing is, I act chill. I joke. But inside, every reply feels like a verdict.

At midnight she wrote, "Sorry, family dinner! Loved it. Again soon?"

Nikita, you want to know how I got your Ira mami to go out with me? Your Mama will tell you, but you have to promise not to laugh.

I was twenty, she was in my accounting class. I replied to every post she put up on the college page. A comment on her rangoli, a comment on her debate prize. I thought I was being subtle.

When I finally asked her for tea at the stall near the gate, I wrote the message on paper first. Changed three words. Sent it.

She took a whole afternoon to reply. I sat in the library pretending to study and felt sick. I was sure she'd say no and tell her friends.

She said yes. Later she told me she'd been at her cousin's wedding all day.

The turning point, Nikita, was sending that message at all. Fear nearly stopped me.

Shankar had been seeing Leela for ten weeks, mostly at the weekly market in their small town in Kerala, where she ran her father's spice stall and he ran the phone repair shop across the lane.

Everyone in the lane had opinions. Thomas from the tea shop kept asking, "So? Is it serious or not?" and Shankar never knew what to say.

On Thursday evening, after the market closed, he helped Leela stack the empty sacks. Then he said, "Leela. I don't want to see anyone else. I'd like it to be just us. What about you?"

She stopped stacking. "You're asking me? Here? Among the sacks?"

"I couldn't wait for a better place."

She laughed. Then she said, "I need to think about it. My father..."

"That's okay. At least now I know you know."

Walking home, he felt oddly light.

At first it was little things. Chinmay, who used to eat anything, learned to order the vegetarian thali when they all went out, because Fatima didn't eat pork and he'd decided to make meals simpler for everyone. Fatima started coming to their Sunday cricket and cheering badly.

Fatima put down her spoon. "My father asked the same thing about you last week."

They looked at each other across the table. Suraj waited for someone to change the subject.

Instead Fatima said, "So we tell them together. Not separately." Chinmay nodded slowly.

Suraj realised they weren't just a couple anymore. They were a team facing something.

Farida and Yusuf were to be married in the winter, and everyone in their kasba near Bhopal agreed it was a good match.

Then Farida was selected for the district health programme. It meant travelling to villages three weeks a month.

She told Yusuf on the bench outside the post office, expecting him to be proud. He was quiet for a long time.

"Three weeks?" he said. "Who will be at home?"

"We will be at home. One week a month. Then we'll see."

"My mother expected..."

"Your mother expected. What do you expect?"

He didn't answer. She felt her face go hot. She had assumed they wanted the same things.

Later, at the tailoring shop, her friend Damini listened and said, "Better you know now how he fights than after the wedding."

Farida thought about that all evening. It wasn't the travel she was worried about. It was that silence.
